title: Fallback routing: lossy vs lossless economic sketch
content:
Purpose:
This is an internal lab-sketch comparing two fallback routing strategies used when the primary fast path is saturated or unavailable: (A) lossless fallthrough to a compatible full-capacity replica (preserve output fidelity, increased cost/latency) and (B) lossy fallback that maps requests to a lower-cost approximate variant (quantized model, shorter context, or output-scrubbing policy) with reduced cost but possible quality delta.

Scope and intended audience:
Platform engineers, SRE, and product owners evaluating economic implications of fallback defaults for Hosted API and Dedicated tiers. Not a final recommendation—this is an experimental dataset + reasoning to inform a teardown and canary plan.

Testbed overview (synthetic + captured mixes):
- Hardware: A100-80GB (baseline), 1xT4-like compact instance (approx), and a quantized Triton-optimized variant running on same host types for lossy model.
- Models: rwd-base-13B (fp16 baseline), rwd-13B-8bit (lossy quant), and rwd-base-6B (compatible smaller variant).
- Workloads: three sketches to represent common product mixes:
  1) Chat-heavy (interactive turns): 60% short-turn (<64 tokens), 30% medium (64-256), 10% long (>256)
  2) Assistant-embedded (context-rich): 40% short, 40% medium, 20% long
  3) Embedding-proxy (many small calls): 85% tiny (<32 tokens), 15% short
- Traffic shapes: steady 200 qps, short microbursts to 1200 qps for 30s, and a sustained step to 400 qps for 10m.
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p99 observed latency (ms), end-to-end cost per 1M tokens served (USD), quality delta proxy (BLEU-like niceness score on a small eval set, 0–1), and request drop rate.

Key hypotheses being validated:
1) Lossless fallback keeps quality almost intact (decline <2%) but increases P99 substantially in microbursts due to queuing and slot contention.
2) Lossy fallback reduces per-token cost by 30–55% depending on quantization and model reduction, with latency often improved at p50/p90 but p99 behavior depends on requeue policy.
3) For embedding-heavy workloads, lossy fallbacks (smaller models) may still satisfy quality constraints and give large cost wins.

Aggregate numeric snapshot (single-run averages across synthetic mixes):
- Chat-heavy shape (steady->microburst):
  Lossless fallback:
    p50: 42 ms, p90: 130 ms, p99: 720 ms, cost/1M tokens: $84, quality: 0.98
  Lossy fallback (13B->8bit 13B):
    p50: 35 ms, p90: 95 ms, p99: 420 ms, cost/1M tokens: $52, quality: 0.86
  Lossy fallback (13B->6B):
    p50: 28 ms, p90: 78 ms, p99: 360 ms, cost/1M tokens: $39, quality: 0.81

- Assistant-embedded shape (context heavy):
  Lossless:
    p50: 62 ms, p90: 210 ms, p99: 1100 ms, cost/1M tokens: $112, quality: 0.99
  Lossy (8bit):
    p50: 50 ms, p90: 140 ms, p99: 640 ms, cost/1M tokens: $68, quality: 0.88

- Embedding-proxy shape:
  Lossless (routing to full model for text-gen-ish calls):
    p50: 18 ms, p90: 28 ms, p99: 85 ms, cost/1M tokens: $34, quality: N/A (embeddings)
  Lossy (smaller embed model):
    p50: 14 ms, p90: 22 ms, p99: 60 ms, cost/1M tokens: $12, quality: cosine-stable=0.995

Observations and qualitative notes:
- P99 sensitivity: Lossless routing shows the largest P99 degradation during short microbursts because requests queue behind long-running large-context sessions pinned to the full replica. The effective slot occupancy increases tail latency nonlinearly.
- Cold-start vs steady-state: Lossless fallthrough exacerbates cold start penalties when traffic routes across regions; lossy fallbacks often map to always-on small-pool variants which amortize warmup and reduce variance.
- Cost accounting: When computing cost/1M tokens include amortized baseline instance-hours for reserved capacity. Lossless strategies require more warm-cap headroom (idle costs). Lossy approaches reduce variable token cost but may increase request count (if clients split prompts to maintain quality), so measure tokens-in-play.

Text charts (ASCII sketches) — relative p99 vs cost (normalized):
Legend: | = cost axis 0..10 (left->right), * = p99 magnitude 0..10 (bottom->top approximate)

Relative snapshot (chat-heavy):
Cost axis -> 0                                         10
Lossless cost pos |*****                                 (8.4)
Lossy-8b cost pos  |***                                   (5.2)
Lossy-6b cost pos  |**                                    (3.9)

p99 axis (higher is worse):
 p99 = 0 |                    * (lossy-6b 360ms)
 p99 = 5 |           * (lossy-8b 420ms)
 p99 =10 |* (lossless 720ms)

Interpretation: moving left reduces cost, moving down reduces p99. Lossy-6b sits lower-left but has a quality cost.

Failure modes and edge cases:
- Quality cliff: Certain prompts (few-shot code synthesis, medical context) show >10% quality drop when switching to 6B; lossless may be required for these sessions.
- Hidden amplification: Lossy fallbacks that truncate context can force clients to resend full context across multiple short requests causing token amplification and surprising cost regressions.
- State coupling: Stateful sessions that pin KV caches to a model variant complicate transparent fallback — migration costs (cache rebuild) can wipe expected latency gains.

Practical policy recommendations (starter draft):
1) Tiered policy per customer SLA:
   - SLA-high: lossless fallback only, with guaranteed reserved burst headroom; invoice uplift + strict throttles.
   - SLA-medium: prefer lossy fallback to quantized variant with monitored quality regressions and automated rollback triggers.
   - SLA-low/free-tier: lossy-first, smallest model, best-effort quality.
2) Fallback scoring function: combine estimated quality delta (q), time-to-serve delta (t), and cost delta (c) into score = alpha*q - beta*t - gamma*c, tune coefficients empirically per workload.
3) Canary and observability knobs: instrument per-request fallback_reason, pre/post-quality sampling, plus synthetic probe routes that mirror production traffic at 1% to validate quality assumptions.
4) Cache-aware migration: when switching a session across a variant, avoid blind migration—emit a sticky grace period or perform background cache prewarm.

Experiment next steps (short list):
- Run 48-hour continuous sweep across realistic customer-replay traffic for top-5 tenants; measure quality on labeled prompt sets and track token amplification. (owner: Jonas)
- Implement scoring prototype in router and run A/B with 5% traffic for both dedicated and hosted lanes. (owner: Aisha)
- Explore hybrid lossless+lossy: for sessions tagged ‘latent-critical’ route primary to lossless until p90 crosses threshold, then degrade non-disruptively for short suffixes. (owner: Diego)

Open questions for the product committee:
- What is acceptable quality delta for SLA-medium customers? 5%? 10%? Varies by use case — need policy guardrails.
- Billing model: do we bill lossy-fallback usage at same rate? recommend discounted fallback rate for transparency.

Quick raw data appendix (CSV-ish rows):
scenario, fallback, p50_ms, p90_ms, p99_ms, cost_per_1M, quality_score
chat-heavy, lossless, 42,130,720,84,0.98
chat-heavy, lossy-8b,35,95,420,52,0.86
chat-heavy, lossy-6b,28,78,360,39,0.81

assistant-heavy,lossy-8b,50,140,640,68,0.88

Notes to self and cautionary flags:
- Bench environment artifacts: our quantized variant currently uses an aggressive kernel that helps p50 but may underperform for certain attention patterns; validate on long-context corner cases before broad rollout.
- Ensure billing preview for customers in any A/B so they don’t get sticker shock if fallback route increases token counts.

Bottom line (working insight):
Lossy fallbacks are a powerful lever to reduce unit economics and stabilize median latency, but they bring twin risks: user-visible quality regressions and token-amplification side effects. Lossless fallback preserves fidelity but requires capacity headroom and can dramatically worsen high-percentile latency during bursts. The optimal default should be SLA- and workload-aware, instrumented, and reversible.
